The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has transformed research practices, economic organization, and civic life. As machine learning systems become embedded in education, medicine, law, and government, scholars require an integrative framework that connects technical capability with social consequence. Existing studies often treat AI either as a narrow engineering problem or as a speculative societal risk, leaving insufficient attention to the institutional processes through which algorithmic decisions are adopted, evaluated, and regulated.

This paper addresses that gap by analyzing AI as a distributed socio-technical system in which models, data, incentives, and governance structures co-evolve. Drawing on computational theory, empirical case studies, and policy analysis, we develop a framework for assessing AI’s impact across three dimensions: capability, accountability, and distribution. The central argument is that the effectiveness of AI interventions depends not only on model performance but also on the transparency, adaptability, and legitimacy of the institutions that deploy them.

The contributions of this paper are threefold. First, we propose a multidimensional taxonomy for classifying AI systems according to autonomy, scope, and reversibility. Second, we identify institutional mechanisms—auditability, human oversight, and contestability—that mediate AI’s effects on public trust. Third, we offer policy implications for designing adaptive governance structures that can accommodate rapid technological change while protecting democratic values. By linking technical development with institutional design, this paper aims to provide a foundation for future research on the responsible integration of artificial intelligence in complex societies.
